items.question: Trace the transformation of the Indian National Congress from a moderate pressure group in 1885 into a mass movement demanding complete independence by 1929.
items.modelAnswer:
The **Indian National Congress**, founded in **1885** by **A.O. Hume** with **W.C. Bonnerjee** as its first president, began as a forum of Western-educated elites seeking reform *within* the British system. This **Moderate phase (1885-1905)** relied on **petitions, resolutions and appeals** — derided as 'political mendicancy' — and its leaders **Dadabhai Naoroji, Gokhale, Surendranath Banerjee and Pherozeshah Mehta** demanded Indianisation of services, council representation and reduced military spending. Naoroji's **Drain of Wealth theory** gave the movement an economic critique that would outlast the Moderates themselves.

The **Partition of Bengal (1905)** by Curzon proved the turning point. It ignited the **Swadeshi and Boycott Movement** and empowered the **Extremists** — the **Lal-Bal-Pal** trio and Aurobindo Ghose — who demanded **Swaraj** and mass action, Tilak declaring 'Swaraj is my birthright'. Ideological differences produced the **Surat Split (1907)**, but the wings reunited at **Lucknow (1916)**, where the **Lucknow Pact** forged Congress-League unity and the **Home Rule Leagues** of Tilak and Besant broadened participation.

The arrival of **Gandhi** converted the Congress into a genuine mass organisation. The **Rowlatt Act and Jallianwala Bagh (1919)** radicalised opinion; the **Non-Cooperation Movement (1920-22)**, merged with the **Khilafat Movement**, drew in peasants, students and women for the first time, and the **Nagpur session (1920)** reorganised the party down to the village. Even the **Swaraj Party (1923)** and the response to the all-British **Simon Commission (1927)** kept the momentum alive. Finally, rejecting the Dominion-Status ceiling of the **Nehru Report (1928)**, the **Lahore Session (1929)** under Jawaharlal Nehru adopted **Purna Swaraj**, fixing **26 January 1930** as Independence Day. Thus, within four decades, a petitioning elite had become a mass-based movement committed to full freedom — a foundation the later Civil Disobedience and Quit India movements would build upon.
keyPoints: 1885 founding (Hume, Bonnerjee); Moderate methods = petitions/resolutions ('political mendicancy').
Moderate leaders (Naoroji, Gokhale, Banerjee, Mehta); Drain of Wealth as lasting economic critique.
1905 Partition of Bengal -> Swadeshi/Boycott and rise of Extremists (Lal-Bal-Pal); Surat Split 1907; Lucknow reunion 1916.
Gandhi's entry: Rowlatt/Jallianwala 1919, Non-Cooperation + Khilafat (1920-22), Nagpur reorganisation.
Simon Commission (1927) and Nehru Report (1928) sharpened demands.
Lahore 1929: Purna Swaraj adopted; 26 January 1930 as first Independence Day.

items.question: Assess the contribution of revolutionary nationalism and Subhas Chandra Bose's Indian National Army to India's freedom struggle. How did these complement the Congress-led movement?
items.modelAnswer:
Alongside the constitutional and mass-movement strands of the freedom struggle ran a **revolutionary tradition** that believed British rule would yield only to force. Growing out of the **Swadeshi agitation (1905)**, Bengal's **Anushilan Samiti** and **Jugantar**, and figures like **Aurobindo Ghose** (*Bande Mataram*, the **Alipore Bomb Case**) and **Khudiram Bose**, gave nationalism a militant edge. Overseas, the **Ghadar Party (1913, USA)** under **Har Dayal, Sohan Singh Bhakna and Rashbehari Bose** planned wartime revolt. In the 1920s the **HSRA** — **Bhagat Singh, Chandrasekhar Azad, Sukhdev, Rajguru** — used dramatic acts such as the Assembly bomb (1929) to 'make the deaf hear'; the **execution of Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev and Rajguru (1931)** created enduring martyrs, condemned even by the Congress at Karachi.

**Subhas Chandra Bose** carried this militant logic to its furthest point. Twice **Congress President (Haripura 1938, Tripuri 1939)**, he broke with the Gandhian mainstream, founded the **Forward Bloc (1939)**, and reorganised the **Indian National Army (Azad Hind Fauj)** with Japanese support, including the **Rani of Jhansi regiment**, rallying Indians with 'Give me blood, and I shall give you freedom'. Though the INA was militarily defeated, the **INA Trials (1945-46)** at the Red Fort — alongside the **RIN Mutiny (1946)** — triggered mass sympathy and convinced the British that even the armed forces were no longer reliable.

These strands **complemented rather than replaced** the Congress movement. While the Congress mobilised millions and negotiated the transfer of power, revolutionaries and the INA **kept pressure on the Raj**, inspired the youth, and demonstrated that Indians would sacrifice for freedom. The regional dimension is striking in **Andhra**, where **Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24)** fused tribal grievance with anti-colonial armed struggle. Together, the moral force of Gandhian mass politics and the sacrificial militancy of the revolutionaries hastened independence in 1947.
keyPoints: Revolutionary roots: Anushilan Samiti/Jugantar, Aurobindo (Bande Mataram, Alipore case), Khudiram Bose.
Ghadar Party (1913, USA) and the HSRA (Bhagat Singh, Azad, Sukhdev, Rajguru); 1931 executions created martyrs.
Bose: Congress President (1938, 1939), resignation, Forward Bloc (1939), INA/Azad Hind Fauj with Rani of Jhansi regiment.
INA Trials (1945-46) and RIN Mutiny (1946) generated mass sympathy and undermined British confidence.
Revolutionaries complemented, not replaced, the Congress by sustaining pressure and inspiring youth.
AP angle: Alluri Sitarama Raju's Rampa Rebellion (1922-24) as regional armed anti-colonial struggle.
